summary: This informational RFC defines an XML schema for managing reverse DNS in a tightly controlled REST environment. It documents a schema that ICANN has run in a RESTful system since 2011, and which registries responsible for reverse delegations use.

plainLanguage.summary: Reverse DNS turns a number back into a name. This describes a standard form for the paperwork used to manage those lookups through a web service.

questions: how to manage reverse dns via rest
subtitle: Standard format for updating reverse DNS through a web service

tldr.problem: Reverse DNS delegations in IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA zones change frequently as organizations roll over DNSSEC keys. Manual processes are slow and error-prone, and there was no standard structured format for these updates.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines two XML schemas for a REST-based HTTPS management service: one for zone updates (PUT/DELETE/GET operations) and one for handling updates that require approval before they take effect. ICANN has run this system since 2011, and regional Internet registries use it to manage their reverse delegations securely.
tldr.outcome: A standardized, secure, and automated way to manage reverse DNS delegations, reducing manual work and supporting secure certificate-based authentication through X.509 certificates.

today: RFC 7745 is an Informational RFC published in January 2016 and has not been obsoleted. ICANN continues to operate the reverse DNS management service described in the RFC, and it is the standard tool used by regional Internet registries to manage reverse delegations.

sections.title: Reverse DNS and DNSSEC
sections.content:
Reverse DNS translates an IP address back into a domain name. For example, looking up the address 192.0.2.1 might return a name like mail.example.com. This lookup happens through the IN-ADDR.ARPA zone for IPv4 and IP6.ARPA for IPv6.

When DNSSEC signing came into wider use, organizations had to update the DNSKEY and DS records in the parent zones (IN-ADDR.ARPA or IP6.ARPA) more often, as DNS keys were rotated or expired. Manually submitting changes by email to regional Internet registries (RIRs) became tedious and prone to error.

ICANN developed this system in response to requests from RIRs to automate these updates. Since 2011, it has been running a REST-based HTTPS service where organizations submit XML documents to change their reverse DNS delegations securely.
sections.plainLanguage: Reverse DNS is like a phone book that works backwards: you give it a number and it tells you whose number it is. When people use new security codes (DNSSEC keys), the phone book has to be updated. This is a standard way to do that update through the Internet instead of by hand.

sections.title: Zone and Queue XML Schemas
sections.content:
The RFC defines two separate XML schemas, both written in RelaxNG Compact notation.

The zone schema is used for GET, PUT, and DELETE operations on active reverse DNS delegations. A zone element contains the zone name (like 10.in-addr.arpa), at least two nameserver entries with fully qualified domain names, and optionally DS records for DNSSEC. Each zone element can include metadata like the IP version, administrative state, and last modification timestamp.

The queue schema is used when updates need approval before they become active. An administrator can submit a change, and the system stores it in a queue. Another authorized party can retrieve the queued entry, review it, and approve it by sending an acknowledgement to a provided URL. Queue entries include the submitted timestamp, the HTTP method used (PUT or DELETE), and a reference URL for approval.

Both schemas support IPv4 (ipv4) and IPv6 (ipv6) address versions through an ipversion attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The schema is like a form with blanks to fill in: the zone name, the nameservers, and security keys. It works the same way whether you are adding a new delegation or removing an old one, and whether it is for IPv4 or IPv6.

sections.title: HTTP Operations and Authentication
sections.content:
Updates are submitted to the service via standard HTTP operations over HTTPS. The URI format is straightforward: https://host.example.org/<ipversion>/<zone>.

GET operations retrieve the current state of a zone or a list of zones. No XML body is required.

PUT operations submit a new zone delegation or replace an existing one. The XML document must be well-formed, and content-length headers are required.

DELETE operations remove a zone delegation. Like PUT, the XML document must be sent with proper headers.

Authentication is handled through X.509 client certificates. Both the client and server present certificates, creating a mutually authenticated, encrypted channel. The system operator issues certificates to organizations, binding each certificate to the delegations that organization is authorized to manage. This approach means no passwords are needed; authentication is cryptographic and automatic.
sections.plainLanguage: You make requests to the web service using standard web commands (GET to look, PUT to add or change, DELETE to remove). Instead of logging in with a password, you use a special certificate that proves who you are.

sections.title: Security Model
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the XML schema itself contains no sensitive data. All information in a zone element is either already published in DNS or available through WHOIS, so the schema does not leak secrets.

Security is provided by the transport layer (HTTPS with TLS), by mutual X.509 certificate authentication, and by the service's authorization logic. The HTTPS layer protects against message modification, insertion, deletion, man-in-the-middle attacks, and replay attacks.

The service operator is responsible for defining which delegations each certificate holder can modify, and for handling denial-of-service protection. Those details are out of scope for the RFC.

The separation of update and approval via out-of-band acknowledgement URLs allows organizations to implement two-person rule policies, where one person submits a change and another must approve it before it takes effect.
sections.plainLanguage: The data itself is not secret, but the connection is encrypted and signed so nobody can sneak in a fake update. The service checks that your certificate says you are allowed to make that change.
